buffers-intro-s1.title: Four mixtures of acetic acid and sodium hydroxide
buffers-intro-s1.text: Each flask starts with 50.0 mL of 0.100 M acetic acid, CH₃COOH (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵). A different volume of 0.100 M NaOH is added to each. Temperature 25 °C.

buffers-intro-s2.title: Four solutions
buffers-intro-s2.html: Key: HF hydrofluoric acid molecule; F⁻ fluoride; H₃O⁺ hydronium; Na⁺ sodium ion; Cl⁻ chloride. Water is not drawn, nor the few H₃O⁺ and F⁻ ions made when HF ionizes.

buffers-intro-s3.title: Two acid-base reactions
buffers-intro-s3.text:
Reaction I: aqueous HF (Ka = 6.8 × 10⁻⁴) is mixed with aqueous NaOH.

Reaction II: aqueous NH₃ (Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) is mixed with aqueous HCl.

items.q: Which flask contains a buffer?
options: Flask 2
Flask 1
Flask 3
Flask 4

why.correct: Flask 2 has 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol acetic acid and 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol NaOH. The OH⁻ converts half the acid to acetate, leaving equal amounts of CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻: a weak acid with its conjugate base.
options: Right: weak acid and conjugate base in similar amounts.
Flask 1 holds only acetic acid; there is no conjugate base to react with added acid.
Flask 3 is exactly neutralized: all the acid became acetate, so there is no weak acid left.
Flask 4 has excess NaOH and no acetic acid left; its pH is set by the strong base.

items.q: What is the pH in Flask 2?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the pH of the acid alone. Let the 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol OH⁻ react with the acid first.
Value: that is the pOH. [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻] gives the pH directly.

why.correct: After reaction: 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COOH and 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COO⁻. In Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA], the volume cancels, so [H₃O⁺] = Ka × (2.50 × 10⁻³)/(2.50 × 10⁻³) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ M and pH = −log(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.74, which is pKa.

items.q: What is the pH in Flask 3?

mistakes.why: Value: 7.00 is the equivalence pH only for a strong acid with a strong base. Here acetate, a weak base, is left in solution.
Value: the volume doubled to 100.0 mL, so [CH₃COO⁻] = 0.0500 M, not 0.100 M.

why.correct: All 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol acid became acetate, now in 100.0 mL: [CH₃COO⁻] = 0.0500 M. Kb = Kw/Ka = 5.56 × 10⁻¹⁰. [OH⁻] = √(5.56 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.0500) = 5.27 × 10⁻⁶ M; pOH = 5.278; pH = 8.72.

items.q: What is the pH in Flask 4?

mistakes.why: Value: divide the excess OH⁻ by the total volume, 110.0 mL, not the 60.0 mL of base.

why.correct: OH⁻ added: 6.00 × 10⁻³ mol; acid: 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol. Excess OH⁻ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol in 0.1100 L = 0.00909 M. The acetate adds very little OH⁻ beside this. pOH = 2.041; pH = 11.96.

items.q: Apart from water and Na⁺, which species is present in the greatest amount in Flask 3?
options: CH₃COO⁻
CH₃COOH
OH⁻
H₃O⁺

why.correct: Every acetic acid molecule reacted with OH⁻, so the flask holds 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COO⁻. Only a tiny amount of it takes a proton back from water.
options: Right: the conjugate base is what remains at equivalence.
Only a trace of CH₃COOH re-forms, about 5 × 10⁻⁶ M.
OH⁻ is present at about 5 × 10⁻⁶ M, made by acetate reacting with water; far less than the acetate.
The solution is basic, so H₃O⁺ is the scarcest of these.

items.q: Which box represents a buffer?
options: P
Q
R
S

why.correct: Box P has a weak acid (HF) and its conjugate base (F⁻) in equal amounts. Added H₃O⁺ reacts with F⁻; added OH⁻ reacts with HF.
options: Right: weak acid plus conjugate base.
Box Q is a strong acid solution with spare Cl⁻. Cl⁻ is too weak a base to remove added H₃O⁺.
Box R has the base F⁻ but no HF to react with added OH⁻.
Box S has the weak acid but no F⁻ to react with added H₃O⁺.

items.q: Box Q contains Cl⁻, the conjugate base of HCl. Why is it not a buffer?
options: Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so it does not take H⁺ from added H₃O⁺
It has more Cl⁻ than H₃O⁺, and a buffer needs equal amounts
Na⁺ ions react with added OH⁻ and use it up
A buffer is a solution with no H₃O⁺ ions

why.correct: HCl ionizes fully, so its conjugate base has a negligible Kb: Cl⁻ does not pick protons back up. Added acid would stay as free H₃O⁺, and the pH would drop sharply.
options: Right: a buffer needs a conjugate base strong enough to react with added acid.
Buffers work over a range of ratios; unequal amounts are not the problem here.
Na⁺ is a spectator ion; it does not react with OH⁻.
Every water solution has some H₃O⁺, buffers included.

items.q: Which box has the highest pH?
options: R
P
Q
S

why.correct: Box R holds only F⁻, a weak base: F⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HF + OH⁻ makes the solution slightly basic. Every other box contains an acid.
options: Right: the conjugate base alone gives a basic solution.
Box P is a buffer at pH = pKa of HF, about 3.2: acidic.
Box Q is a strong acid solution, the lowest pH of the four.
Box S is HF alone, a weak acid: acidic.

items.q: Two OH⁻ ions (from NaOH) are added to Box P. Which shows the solutes after reaction?
options: 2 HF, 6 F⁻, 6 Na⁺
4 HF, 4 F⁻, 6 Na⁺, 2 OH⁻
6 HF, 2 F⁻, 6 Na⁺
2 HF, 4 F⁻, 4 Na⁺, 2 H₂O

why.correct: OH⁻ + HF → F⁻ + H₂O goes to completion: two HF become two F⁻, and the two Na⁺ added with the OH⁻ stay as spectators.
options: Right: two HF used, two F⁻ made, six Na⁺ in all.
The OH⁻ cannot stay free beside HF: it reacts with the weak acid.
The change goes the wrong way: OH⁻ removes HF and makes F⁻.
This loses two F⁻ and the Na⁺ added with the base; ions are not destroyed.

items.q: Which mixtures, dissolved in 1.0 L of water, make a buffer? Select all that apply.
options: 0.20 mol HNO₂ and 0.15 mol NaNO₂
0.20 mol HNO₃ and 0.15 mol NaNO₃
0.20 mol NH₃ and 0.10 mol HCl
0.20 mol NH₃ and 0.20 mol HCl
0.20 mol NaOH and 0.10 mol HCl

why.correct: A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) together. HNO₂/NO₂⁻ qualifies directly; NH₃ + half as much HCl leaves 0.10 mol NH₃ and 0.10 mol NH₄⁺.
options: Right: weak acid and conjugate base.
HNO₃ is strong; NO₃⁻ cannot remove added acid.
Right: partial neutralization of a weak base makes NH₃/NH₄⁺.
Equal moles convert all NH₃ to NH₄⁺; no weak base remains.
Strong base and strong acid leave only excess NaOH.

items.q: Which is the net ionic equation for Reaction I?
options: HF(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → F⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → 2 H₂O(l)
HF(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaF(aq) + H₂O(l)
H⁺(aq) + F⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → F⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)

why.correct: HF is weak, so it is mostly molecules and is written whole. NaOH is a strong electrolyte, so it appears as OH⁻ with Na⁺ cancelled as a spectator.
options: Right: weak acid written as a molecule.
This is the net equation for a strong acid; HF is not ionized enough to write it as H₃O⁺.
This is the molecular equation; it still shows the spectator Na⁺ inside NaOH and NaF.
This splits HF into ions as if it were strong.

items.q: What is K for the net reaction HF(aq) + OH⁻(aq) ⇌ F⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)? Give your answer in scientific notation.

mistakes.why: Value: this reaction is HF ionizing (Ka) plus the reverse of water ionizing (1/Kw). Multiply Ka by 1/Kw: K = Ka / Kw.
Value: that is Kb of F⁻, the reverse of this reaction. Here K = Ka / Kw = 1/Kb.

why.correct: HF + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + F⁻ (Ka) plus H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ ⇌ 2 H₂O (1/Kw) gives the net reaction, so K = Ka/Kw = (6.8 × 10⁻⁴)/(1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 6.8 × 10¹⁰. So large that the reaction goes essentially to completion.

items.q: Equal moles of NH₃ and HCl react in Reaction II. Which describes the final solution?
options: Acidic, because NH₄⁺ gives protons to water
Neutral, because equal moles of acid and base reacted
Basic, because NH₃ is a base
Neutral, because Cl⁻ is a spectator ion

why.correct: The product NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of a weak base: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺ (Ka = Kw/Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰), so the solution is slightly acidic.
options: Right: the conjugate acid of a weak base is a weak acid.
Equal moles give a neutral solution only for strong acid with strong base.
All the NH₃ was converted to NH₄⁺; no base is left.
Cl⁻ is a spectator, but NH₄⁺ is not: it reacts with water.

items.q: In Reaction II, a small amount of HCl (less than the moles of NH₃) is added to an NH₃ solution. Predict the change in each quantity.

variables.name: Moles of NH₃
variables.why: H₃O⁺ + NH₃ → NH₄⁺ + H₂O uses up ammonia, one for one with the acid added.

variables.name: Moles of NH₄⁺
variables.why: Each H₃O⁺ that reacts makes one NH₄⁺.

variables.name: Kb of NH₃
variables.why: Kb is an equilibrium constant and changes only with temperature, not with what is added.

variables.name: pH
variables.why: Less base and more of its conjugate acid: the pH falls, though only a little once NH₄⁺ is present.

why.correct: Added acid converts the weak base into its conjugate acid; the mixture of NH₃ and NH₄⁺ is a buffer.

items.q: A solution contains 0.30 M HNO₂ and 0.20 M NaNO₂ (Ka of HNO₂ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴). What is its pH?

mistakes.why: Value: the ratio is upside down. [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻], with the acid on top.
Value: you ignored the NO₂⁻. It is already present at 0.20 M, so use [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [HNO₂]/[NO₂⁻].

why.correct: Rearrange Ka = [H₃O⁺][NO₂⁻]/[HNO₂]: [H₃O⁺] = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.30/0.20 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ M. pH = −log(6.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.22. Both amounts barely change, because the NO₂⁻ already present pushes the ionization of HNO₂ even further left.

items.q: A flask holds 0.0400 mol of acetic acid. What volume of 0.500 M NaOH, in mL, converts exactly half of it to acetate?

mistakes.why: Value: that converts all of the acid. Half the acid needs 0.0200 mol OH⁻.

why.correct: Half of 0.0400 mol is 0.0200 mol; 0.0200 mol ÷ 0.500 mol/L = 0.0400 L = 40.0 mL. The flask then holds 0.0200 mol each of acid and acetate.

items.q: A student mixes 0.020 mol NH₃ and 0.010 mol HCl in water to make 0.500 L of solution. Kb of NH₃ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. What is the pH?

mistakes.why: Value: that is pKb, so it is really the pOH. For a base buffer use the Ka of NH₄⁺ (Kw/Kb) for pH, or subtract the pOH from 14.00.

why.correct: H₃O⁺ + NH₃ → NH₄⁺ leaves 0.010 mol NH₃ and 0.010 mol NH₄⁺. For NH₄⁺, Ka = Kw/Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰. [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [NH₄⁺]/[NH₃] = 5.56 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 1 = 5.56 × 10⁻¹⁰ M → pH = 9.26 (rounding Ka to 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ first gives 9.25, also accepted).

items.q: Equal moles of HCN (Ka = 6.2 × 10⁻¹⁰) and KOH are mixed. How does the final pH compare with 7?
options: Above 7, because CN⁻ takes protons from water
Equal to 7, because the acid and base were in equal moles
Below 7, because HCN is an acid
Equal to 7, because K⁺ is a spectator ion

why.correct: All the HCN becomes CN⁻, the conjugate base of a very weak acid. CN⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCN + OH⁻ (Kb = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵) makes the solution basic.
options: Right: a weak acid neutralized by a strong base leaves a basic solution.
Equal moles give pH 7 only when both are strong.
No HCN remains after it reacts with an equal amount of KOH.
K⁺ is a spectator, but CN⁻ is not.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the pH after a strong base is added to a weak acid in order.
options: Find the moles of weak acid and of OH⁻ added
Let OH⁻ react with the weak acid to completion; record what is left
Decide the case: acid and conjugate base left (a buffer), only conjugate base left, or excess OH⁻
Use the matching equation: Ka ratio, Kb of the conjugate base, or excess OH⁻ over total volume

why.correct: The neutralization runs first because its K is huge. What remains decides which equilibrium sets the pH.

items.q: A buffer contains 0.20 mol NH₃ and 0.20 mol NH₄Cl. A student adds 0.050 mol of HCl. Which reaction takes place?
options: NH₃ + H₃O⁺ → NH₄⁺ + H₂O
NH₄⁺ + H₃O⁺ → NH₅²⁺ + H₂O
NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O
Cl⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HCl + H₂O

why.correct: Added acid is taken up by the base of the pair, NH₃, which becomes NH₄⁺. Free H₃O⁺ stays low.
options: Right: the weak base removes the added acid.
NH₄⁺ already carries a positive charge and has no lone pair to accept another proton.
This is how the buffer handles added base, not added acid.
Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and does not take protons.
